steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper investigating latent "affective bias" (biased emotion associations toward gender, race and religion groups) in large pre-trained language models used for textual emotion detection. Motivate the problem, define affective bias with examples, state the research question and our approach, and give the paper outline.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- PLMs are deployed everywhere, but learn social stereotypes from human-written data
- What affective bias is, with examples
- Where affective bias comes from and why it is harmful
- Our study: research question, corpus level and prediction level analysis
- Paper organization

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Recently, large scale Natural Language Processing (NLP) models are being deployed more and more in real-world applications in almost all domains, like health-care, business, legal systems, etc. This is because they are effective at making data-driven decisions and can understand natural language even better than humans. Transformer based large Pre-trained Language Models (PLMs) have been very influential in NLP because they can generate powerful contextual representations. PLMs are mostly built with a self-supervised learning strategy that relies heavily on unlabelled data, which is abundantly available from the deluge of human generated data. But this historical textual data has its roots in human thought, so it often reflects latent social stereotypes. For example, the Social Role Theory by Eagly et al. shows that gender stereotypes develop from what perceivers observe: they associate the capabilities and personality attributes of different genders with the activities these genders do in their day-to-day lives over time. This builds rigid stereotypes in human minds and in their writings about how these genders behave (e.g. women are highly emotional), where they work (e.g. women preferred in children's daycare), etc. So the data from these human generated data repositories ends up passing on these stereotypes as linguistic biases through NLP algorithms, especially the ones built on large PLMs that use huge amounts of data.

Along these lines, investigating "Affective Bias" in NLP is a recent stream of research. It studies whether there is any unfair/biased association of emotions (anger, fear, joy, etc.) or sentiments (positive, negative, etc.) with underrepresented or protected groups in a domain, which may lead affective computing systems like sentiment or emotion detection systems to give unfavorable outcomes for these protected groups. For example, a model that consistently associates women with a different class of emotion, or with the same emotion but a different emotion intensity compared to its predictions for male, could be seen as showing affective bias. In the same way, always associating a particular religion with a specific emotion is affective bias too. A real world case of affective bias is the Google sentiment analyzer judging that being gay is bad, by giving high negative sentiments to sentences like 'I'm a gay black woman', 'I'm a homosexual', etc. To make affective bias easier to understand, table 1 shows a sample set of affectively biased emotion predictions from the PLM based textual emotion detection models we built in this study for affective bias analysis (the models are explained in detail in section 4.1). The first set in the table shows affective bias from differences in predicted emotion classes, and the second set shows affective bias from differences in predicted emotion intensities.

  - also model/algorithmic design treatment of protected attributes (cite)
  - harms: unfair decisions, denying opportunities/resources, false portrayal of marginalized groups

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Recently, large scale Natural Language Processing (NLP) models are being deployed more and more in real-world applications in almost all domains, like health-care, business, legal systems, etc. This is because they are effective at making data-driven decisions and can understand natural language even better than humans. Transformer based large Pre-trained Language Models (PLMs) have been very influential in NLP because they can generate powerful contextual representations. PLMs are mostly built with a self-supervised learning strategy that relies heavily on unlabelled data, which is abundantly available from the deluge of human generated data. But this historical textual data has its roots in human thought, so it often reflects latent social stereotypes. For example, the Social Role Theory by Eagly et al. shows that gender stereotypes develop from what perceivers observe: they associate the capabilities and personality attributes of different genders with the activities these genders do in their day-to-day lives over time. This builds rigid stereotypes in human minds and in their writings about how these genders behave (e.g. women are highly emotional), where they work (e.g. women preferred in children's daycare), etc. So the data from these human generated data repositories ends up passing on these stereotypes as linguistic biases through NLP algorithms, especially the ones built on large PLMs that use huge amounts of data.

Along these lines, investigating "Affective Bias" in NLP is a recent stream of research. It studies whether there is any unfair/biased association of emotions (anger, fear, joy, etc.) or sentiments (positive, negative, etc.) with underrepresented or protected groups in a domain, which may lead affective computing systems like sentiment or emotion detection systems to give unfavorable outcomes for these protected groups. For example, a model that consistently associates women with a different class of emotion, or with the same emotion but a different emotion intensity compared to its predictions for male, could be seen as showing affective bias. In the same way, always associating a particular religion with a specific emotion is affective bias too. A real world case of affective bias is the Google sentiment analyzer judging that being gay is bad, by giving high negative sentiments to sentences like 'I'm a gay black woman', 'I'm a homosexual', etc. To make affective bias easier to understand, table 1 shows a sample set of affectively biased emotion predictions from the PLM based textual emotion detection models we built in this study for affective bias analysis (the models are explained in detail in section 4.1). The first set in the table shows affective bias from differences in predicted emotion classes, and the second set shows affective bias from differences in predicted emotion intensities.

Like other general algorithmic biases such as gender bias, racial bias, etc., one possible stimulus for affective biases is latent emotion based stereotypes about different social groups in the data. Studies report that this kind of emotion based stereotyping influences how emotions are socialized, which leads to stereotypes spreading, like women's (or men's) experience and expressions being aligned with fear and sadness (or anger and pride). In the same way, affective bias in systems could lead to black women being associated more with the emotion anger when emotions are considered together with the domains race and gender. Besides biased data, another reason for bias is how the model/algorithmic design considers or treats the underrepresented or protected attributes in a domain. Like any other general social biases, these affective biases make textual affective computing systems generate unfair or biased decisions when deployed in the real world, which can harm their utility for socially marginalized populations by denying them opportunities/resources or by portraying these groups falsely. So understanding affective bias in NLP is very important for achieving algorithmic fairness and protecting the socio-political and moral equality of marginalized groups.

In this context, we present an extensive experimental analysis to understand and show the existence of latent "Affective Bias" in transformer based large pre-trained language models for the downstream task of textual emotion detection. Our research question is: Do predictions made by large PLM based textual emotion detection systems systematically or consistently exemplify 'Affective Bias' towards demographic groups? Our investigation mainly aims to identify whether gender, racial, and religious affective biases exist in large PLMs, and we leave the task of affective bias mitigation for future work. First we explore corpus level affective bias, or affect imbalance in the corpus, to find any biased emotion associations in the large scale corpora used to pre-train and fine-tune the PLMs. We do this by analyzing the distribution of emotions or their associations with demographic target terms (e.g., Islam, Quran) related to a social group (e.g., Muslim) in a domain (e.g., Religion). After that we explore prediction level affective bias in four popular transformer based PLMs, BERT (Bidirectional Encoder Representation from Transformers), OpenAI GPT-2 (Generative Pre-trained Transformer), XLNet, and T5 (Text-to-Text Transfer Transformer), which are fine-tuned on a popular corpus SemEval-2018 EI-oc for the task of textual emotion detection. To quantify prediction level affective bias, we run an extensive set of class-based and intensity-based evaluations on the PLMs using three different evaluation corpora, EEC, BITS and CSP. Figure 1 shows a detailed sketch of the overall analysis.

The rest of the paper is organized like this. Section 2 gives the related works. Section 3 gives the corpus level affective bias analysis with its methodology and results. Section 4 gives the exploration of prediction level affective bias, with details on how we built the PLM based textual emotion detection model, the methodology of analysis, and the results. Section 5 discusses the overall results and section 6 gives the conclusions.

But since this historical textual data has its roots in human thought, it often reflects latent social stereotypes [6,7]. For example, the Social Role Theory by Eagly et al. [8] demonstrates that gender stereotypes develop from perceivers' observations, which associate the capabilities and personality attributes of different genders with the activities they engage in in their day-to-day lives over time, building rigid stereotypes in human minds and writings about how these genders behave (e.g. women are highly emotional), where they work (e.g. women preferred in children's daycare), etc. Hence the data from such human generated data repositories eventually convey these stereotypes as linguistic biases through NLP algorithms, especially those built on large PLMs that utilize huge amounts of data [6].

In this direction, the investigation of "Affective Bias" in NLP is a recent stream of research studying the existence of any unfair/biased association of emotions (anger, fear, joy, etc.) or sentiments (positive, negative, etc.) towards underrepresented or protected groups in a domain, which may lead affective computing systems such as sentiment or emotion detection systems to deliver unfavorable outcomes for these protected groups [9]. For instance, a model consistently associating women with a different class of emotion, or with the same emotion at a different intensity compared to predictions for male [10], could be seen as a manifestation of affective bias. Similarly, always associating a particular religion with a specific emotion [11] represents affective bias too. A real world example of affective bias is the Google sentiment analyzer judging that being gay is bad by assigning high negative sentiments to sentences such as 'I'm a gay black woman', 'I'm a homosexual', etc. For better understandability, table 1 illustrates a sample set of affectively biased emotion predictions from the PLM based textual emotion detection models constructed in this study for affective bias analysis (the models are explained in detail in section 4.1). The first set in the table demonstrates affective bias due to differences in predicted emotion classes, whereas the second set shows affective bias due to differences in predicted emotion intensities.

Similar to other general algorithmic biases like gender bias, racial bias, etc., a possible stimulus for affective biases is the latent emotion based stereotypes about different social groups in the data. Studies report that such emotion based stereotyping influences the socialization of emotions, leading to the propagation of stereotypes such as associating women's (or men's) experience and expressions with fear and sadness (or anger and pride) [12]. Similarly, affective bias within systems could facilitate a higher association of black women with the emotion anger when considering emotions with the domains race and gender [13]. In addition to biased data, another reason for bias is how the model/algorithmic design considers or treats the underrepresented or protected attributes concerning a domain [14]. Like any other general social biases, these affective biases make textual affective computing systems generate unfair or biased decisions that can harm their utility towards socially marginalized populations, by denying opportunities/resources or by falsely portraying these groups when deployed in the real world. Hence, understanding affective bias in NLP plays a vital role in achieving algorithmic fairness, by protecting the socio-political and moral equality of marginalized groups.

In this context, we present an extensive experimental analysis to understand and illustrate the existence of latent "Affective Bias" in transformer based large pre-trained language models with respect to the downstream task of textual emotion detection. We set our research question as: Do predictions made by large PLM based textual emotion detection systems systematically or consistently exemplify 'Affective Bias' towards demographic groups? Our investigation primarily aims to identify the existence of gender, racial, and religious affective biases in large PLMs, setting aside affective bias mitigation for future work. We start by exploring corpus level affective bias, or affect imbalance in corpus, to find any biased emotion associations in the large scale corpora used to pre-train and fine-tune the PLMs, analyzing the distribution of emotions or their associations with demographic target terms (e.g., Islam, Quran) related to a social group (e.g., Muslim) concerning a domain (e.g., Religion). Later, we explore prediction level affective bias in four popular transformer based PLMs, BERT (Bidirectional Encoder Representation from Transformers) [15], OpenAI GPT-2 (Generative Pre-trained Transformer) [16], XLNet [17], and T5 (Text-to-Text Transfer Transformer) [18], fine-tuned on the popular corpus SemEval-2018 EI-oc [19] for the task of textual emotion detection. To quantify prediction level affective bias, we subject the PLMs to an extensive set of class-based and intensity-based evaluations using three different evaluation corpora, EEC [20], BITS [21] and CSP [22].
